 Indonesian fire emissions third highest on record this year, says EU’s Copernicus 
 Indonesian fire emissions third highest on record this year, says EU’s Copernicus 
 19-Nov-2026, 12:04 19 Nov 2026, 12:04 Reuters Share The Indonesian archipelago has suffered its worst wildfire season in years, driven by excessively dry super-El Niño weather conditions and warmer temperatures, as well as extensive land clearing.
 Data showed that fires may have damaged nearly 8.9 million hectares, or 4.7% of Indonesia’s land area, this year, well above the 2012–2025 average of 1.9%. (EPA Images pic) 
 SINGAPORE : This year’s fires in Indonesia produced nearly 200 million metric tons of carbon emissions by Nov 15, the European Union’s climate monitoring service said on Thursday, the third-highest annual volume on record. 
 The archipelago has suffered its worst wildfire season in years, driven by excessively dry super-El Niño weather conditions and warmer temperatures, as well as extensive land clearing.
 Total fire emissions fell short of the record of nearly 400 million tons in 2015 and were also slightly lower than in 2006, another strong El Niño year, according to the EU’s Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service (CAMS), which tracks fire emission records dating back to 2003.
 This year’s fire emissions were the equivalent of more than a fifth of Indonesia’s total carbon footprint in 2025, with the country’s energy consumption and industry responsible for an estimated 960 million tons of CO2 last year, according to the Statistical Review of World Energy.
 Emissions generated by Indonesia’s fires were also around the same as the entire energy and industrial carbon footprint of Pakistan last year.
 CAMS data showed that nearly 8.9 million hectares of land could have been damaged by fire in Indonesia this year, 4.7% of its total area, significantly higher than the 2012 to 2025 average of 1.9%.
 The figure is significantly higher than the 2.9-million-hectare estimate for January to October provided last week by geomonitoring platform Nusantara Atlas, which uses a more conservative methodology.
 Though El Niño-driven drought was a decisive factor in this year’s fires, experts have also emphasised the role played by climate change in driving up temperatures.
 Poor land management and the excessive draining of peatland to make way for palm oil or pulpwood concessions have also made Indonesia more vulnerable to fire.
